sections.h2: The Clerk and Recorder's role in a sale
sections.html:
When a house sells in Arapahoe County, the Clerk and Recorder is the office that takes in the signed deed and any mortgage. Filing the deed puts the new owner's name in the public record. It is also the point where Colorado's documentary fee gets paid. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102, whoever hands over a deed or other title-conveying instrument for recording pays the fee to the county clerk and recorder, on top of the normal recording charges.

This office is separate from the treasurer and the assessor. It neither bills property tax nor sets values. Its job in your sale is narrow: accept the signed deed, confirm it can be recorded, collect the fee and add the document to the public record. Call before you send anything, and ask which forms of payment the office takes.

The state charges one cent for every $100 of consideration, rounding a major fraction of $100 up to a full unit. If the total consideration is $500 or less, nothing is due. For a typical house sale, think of it as ten cents per $1,000 of price. Your title company calculates the exact figure and prints it on the settlement statement.

Consideration can be larger than the contract price. The statute counts liens and encumbrances and required charges in the base, so ask how your closing agent figured it. If a single deal covers property in more than one county, each county collects only its share, based on the consideration attributable to the land there, and the person recording the instrument divides the total among the counties.

The county sets the per-document recording charge separately, and that amount is not covered here. Ask the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder for the current figure.

sections.h2: Residential or not: how Colorado decides
sections.html:
Colorado treats a property as residential unless the deed carries a conspicuous statement that it is not to be regarded as residential. The statement has to be on the instrument when it is signed, and cannot be added afterward.

  • Residential: consideration is the amount shown on the conveyance document. If that amount is missing or $500 or less, and a declaration was filed under section 39-14-102, the total sales price on the declaration is used.
  • Commercial or industrial: the full sales price is treated as paid for the real property, unless separate consideration for personal property appears on the use tax return or declaration.
  • Supporting evidence is neither recorded nor made public. The clerk hands it to the county assessor, who keeps it confidential.

That confidentiality is why a recorded deed can show a fee without laying out every detail of the price. The assessor can still see what the property sold for.

sections.h2: Which recorder handles an Aurora, Glendale or Centennial home
sections.html:
The county where the parcel sits decides the recorder. Aurora spreads across Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties. Of its 386,261 residents in 2020, 336,035 lived in Arapahoe, so most Aurora homes are recorded here, but a house in the Adams or Douglas portion is not.

Glendale is an exclave of Arapahoe County surrounded by Denver, and its deeds still go to Arapahoe. Centennial, formed in 2001 out of unincorporated Arapahoe County, is also an Arapahoe city.

CityWhere the deed is recorded
Littleton (county seat)Arapahoe County
CentennialArapahoe County
EnglewoodArapahoe County
Glendale (surrounded by Denver)Arapahoe County
Aurora, Arapahoe portionArapahoe County
Aurora, Adams or Douglas portionAdams or Douglas County

Arapahoe County was one of Colorado's 17 original counties, organized in 1861, and it once covered a much larger area. Adams County was cut from part of it in 1901, with the formal start delayed until November 15, 1902. A deed for land now in Adams County may therefore carry old Arapahoe County references.

Working from an inherited paper file? Find the parcel's current county instead of trusting the county named in an older document. Cities have shifted too: Centennial did not exist before 2001, and Aurora began as Fletcher in 1891 before taking the Aurora name in 1928. Verify the county from the parcel record, not the city in a mailing address.

sections.h2: Check these before the deed is recorded
sections.html:
Three things change the fee or send a document to the wrong office: the consideration, the classification and the county.

  • The price stated on the deed, and whether liens or required charges are counted in it.
  • Whether the deed says the property is not residential. Silence means residential.
  • Which county holds the parcel, especially for Aurora.
  • Whether more than one county is involved, in which case the person recording splits the consideration.
  • A copy of the recorded deed once it comes back, for your files.

The non-residential statement cannot be added to a signed document later, so raise any classification question before you sign. Your title or escrow company can explain how it handles the fee at closing.

Here is the usual order of events when a house sells. You and the buyer sign the contract, and the title company opens an order and researches the parcel. Near closing, you sign the deed, and the closing agent works out the documentary fee from the consideration. The agent then delivers the deed to the Clerk and Recorder, which records it. Once the deed is recorded, the sale is public and funds are released.

If you owe back property tax, the title company pays it from your proceeds, so the recording office is not where that gets settled. Taxes go to the treasurer. The recorder only handles the deed itself. Bring a government photo ID to the signing, and keep copies of the contract, the settlement statement and the recorded deed together in one folder. If anything about the price, the lien payoffs or the property classification looks off on the settlement statement, ask the closing agent to explain it before you sign, because changing a deed after it is recorded is far harder than fixing it first.

A cash buyer follows the same recording steps. What changes is the timeline: with no lender, there is no loan underwriting to wait for, so a clean closing date is easier to hold when you are relocating for a job or settling an estate.

sections.h2: Selling in a county that stretches across the metro area
sections.html:
Arapahoe County mixes some of the densest suburbs on the Front Range with open plains, so sellers rarely face the same situation twice. It runs about 72 miles long and only a few miles wide in places. Strasburg, Deer Trail and Byers on the east side have their own school districts, while the west side splits among Littleton, Englewood, Sheridan and Cherry Creek.

  • Confirm the county before you choose a recorder or treasurer.
  • Ask the title company for the recording instructions it will follow.
  • Budget for the documentary fee in addition to recording charges.
  • Keep the closing statement, since the assessor receives sale details from the clerk.

faqs.q: What is the documentary fee in Colorado?
faqs.a: One cent per $100 of consideration, or ten cents per $1,000. Nothing is owed on $500 or less. It is paid when the deed is offered for recording.

faqs.q: Who collects the documentary fee in Arapahoe County?
faqs.a: The Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder collects it when a deed or other title-conveying instrument is offered for recording.

faqs.q: Is my deed treated as residential or commercial?
faqs.a: Residential by default. It counts as non-residential only if the deed says so conspicuously at signing.

faqs.q: Do Aurora houses always record in Arapahoe County?
faqs.a: No. Aurora lies in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties, and a deed is recorded in the county where the parcel is located.

faqs.q: Where can I get the current per-document recording fee?
faqs.a: Ask the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder directly, since the amount can change.
